paras: The threatened lynching of Fletcher Hollis was an armed manhunt near Smyrna, Delaware, in August 1903, in which posses hunted Hollis, a young Black man accused of shooting Constable James D. Wright at Clayton on August 3, and declared he would be shot if caught. Hollis escaped, Wright recovered, and Hollis was captured in Maryland in February 1904 and sentenced to five years, the pillory and a fine. Dispatches announced that Delaware was "on the eve of another lynching," and a Wilmington editorial tied the hunt to a recent burning in New Castle County.

Constables Wright of Clayton and Charles H. Jones of Smyrna were trying to arrest Hollis, variously aged twenty to twenty-three, on charges of shooting at a man in Dover and disturbing the Friendship colored camp meeting. Wright, about fifty, was a Democratic politician in Kent County.

The constables found Hollis that evening near the Clayton railroad station by the Stockle Hotel, talking with a group of Black people. When Wright told him he was wanted, Hollis drew a revolver and shot him in the abdomen, then ran toward Smyrna holding pursuers off with his pistol.

Posses formed that night under Smyrna Chief of Police Benjamin Turner, Policeman Joseph Cummins and Constable Jones, with W. D. Venn and William King of Clayton. Their strength was given as 300 men in three posses, over 200, over 100, or two parties of about 100 patrolling the Smyrna River to Bombay Hook. According to the New-York Tribune they would "shoot to kill without asking questions," and a Wilmington dispatch said they would not let State Detective Francis take Hollis into custody.

On August 4 Governor Hunn offered a $100 reward and sent state detectives, reportedly insisting "there be no lynching this time." Officers suspected that Black friends had hidden Hollis, and the search turned on Smyrna's Black quarter, whose residents locked their doors and kept off the streets. The following Saturday night, detectives and armed men entered three Black households at "Irishtown" with warrants, finding nothing. Two Black men were held as suspects and released, and Hollis's brothers in Chester, Pennsylvania, said they did not "uphold him in the shooting."

A grand jury indicted Hollis in November 1903; the Smyrna Times noted he had escaped "although a mob hunted him." Robert Coursey of Centreville, Maryland, lodged him in Dover jail on February 27, 1904, where he admitted shooting Wright but denied trying to kill Jones. In April he pleaded guilty and Judge Spruance sentenced him to five years, an hour in the pillory, and $500 and costs. No report of charges against any posse member appears in the coverage.

The first telegraph ran on August 4 as "HUNTED BY THREE POSSES" in the New-York Tribune, "Three Posses Threaten to Lynch Negro" in the New York Herald and "LYNCH LAW FEVER" in the Alexandria Gazette. A shorter Associated Press version ran in the Raleigh News & Observer and the Milford Chronicle, and the Atlanta Constitution printed the Wilmington dispatch on August 10 as "DETERMINED TO KILL NEGRO." These reports called Hollis a "desperado" and relayed the posses' threats without comment.

Delaware papers differed in tone. The Wilmington Evening Journal's editorial "Heaping the Faggots" warned that "this spirit of lynch law has gone entirely too far," yet its news columns the next day headlined the "Tendency of Negroes to Shoot." The Smyrna Times, reprinted in the Middletown Transcript, wrote matter-of-factly that he would have been dealt with "if not trung up to the nearest tree." The Virginia Citizen cited the hunt as proof that lynching had spread north.
The only Black-press item found was a one-sentence wire brief in the Cleveland Gazette on August 8 calling Hollis "a negro desperado," with nothing on the posses.

All accounts of the shooting come from officers or white papers and differ in detail: Wright either seized Hollis or merely touched his shoulder before the shot. The threatened death also varies, from shooting on sight to hanging and, in a March 1904 retrospective, burning.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Fletcher Hollis
bases: Armed posses of 100 to 300 men hunted Hollis, a Black man accused of shooting a constable, and declared they would shoot or lynch him, but never caught him; the force used was threat and searches of Black homes (A1, A4, A14, A24).

The shooting, the escape and the armed posses' threat to kill Hollis are reported independently by the New-York Tribune telegraph, a Wilmington dispatch, the Wilmington Evening Journal and the local Smyrna Times (A1, A4, A5, A13, A14).

accounts.label: Smyrna telegraph (New-York Tribune, New York Herald, Alexandria Gazette)
accounts.gist: Neither constable was armed; Wright seized Hollis and tried to turn the pistol away before Hollis fired; three posses of 300 would shoot him if they caught him.

accounts.label: Local paper (Smyrna Times)
accounts.gist: Wright laid a hand on Hollis's shoulder near the Clayton station and Hollis fired at once; a posse of over 100 searched the creek; officers believed Black friends disguised him as a woman.

accounts.label: Wilmington dispatch
accounts.gist: Two parties of about 100 men patrolled the Smyrna River and said they would not allow the state detective to take Hollis into custody.

accounts.label: Hollis's own statements (via officers and court)
accounts.gist: He admitted shooting Wright but said he did not try to kill the Smyrna constable, and at sentencing sought to say he had not intended to kill Wright.

accounts.label: Hollis's brothers
accounts.gist: They did not uphold the shooting, said Fletcher had not lived in Chester, and feared 'a bad fight' if he were taken with his gun.

accounts.label: Black press wire brief
accounts.gist: Wright was shot by Hollis, 'a negro desperado', who escaped; nothing on the posses.

framing.detail: New York and Washington-area papers ran the Smyrna telegraph as 'HUNTED BY THREE POSSES', 'Three Posses Threaten to Lynch Negro' and 'LYNCH LAW FEVER', calling Hollis a 'desperado' and the lynching 'conceded'.
Wilmington Evening Journal editorial 'Heaping the Faggots' hoped the crowds would not carry out their threat and tied the hunt to the recent burning in New Castle county.
The same paper's news columns headlined the 'Tendency of Negroes to Shoot' and generalized that Black people were 'armed continually' while reporting the governor's opposition to a lynching.
The Smyrna Times reported that he would have been 'severely dealt with, if not trung up' without comment and later called him dangerous to leave at large.
The Virginia Citizen used the Delaware hunt to argue that lynching had spread north, while blaming 'outlaws' of the race.
The Cleveland Gazette ran a one-sentence wire brief calling Hollis 'a negro desperado' with no mention of the posses.

conflicts.note: The local Smyrna Times (over 100) and the Wilmington dispatch (two of about 100) are closer to the scene than the 300 of the first-night telegraph.

record_check.record: Fletcher Hollis; James D. Wright; Constable James D. Wright
record_check.dossier: Fletcher Hollis is the target of the posses; Constable James D. Wright is the white officer Hollis was accused of shooting and is listed twice. Victims should be Fletcher Hollis (and, collectively, Black residents of Smyrna whose homes were searched).
threatened: posses declared they would shoot or lynch him but never had him in hand; he escaped.
The shooting was at Clayton; the posses formed at Smyrna and Clayton and searched Smyrna and the river to Bombay Hook. Wilmington is only a dateline.
Posses led by Smyrna Chief of Police Benjamin Turner, Policeman Joseph Cummins, Constable Charles H. Jones, and W. D. Venn and William King of Clayton.

record_check.record: accused of shooting at a man in Dover and creating a disturbance at a Friendship (colored) camp meeting
record_check.dossier: Those were the charges for the attempted arrest; the accusation driving the posses was shooting Constable Wright.
Also an armed night raid with warrants on three Black households at 'Irishtown' and a search of the Black quarter.
Wright was wounded by Hollis in the precipitating shooting, not by the posses; his race is not stated but implied.

record_check.record: Two posses of about one hundred men each ... he would probably be shot if caught.
record_check.dossier: Accurate for August 4 but omits the outcome: no lynching, indictment, capture at Centreville, Md., in February 1904 and sentence of five years, pillory and fine in April 1904.

info: Shooting of Constable Wright and start of the manhunt on the evening of Monday, August 3, 1903; posses searched through at least August 5, with an armed house search the following Saturday night.

Shooting in front of the Stockle (Stoeckle) Hotel near the Delaware railroad station at Clayton, one mile from Smyrna; the hunt covered Smyrna, its Black quarter and the Smyrna River banks and marshes from Clayton to Bombay Hook.
Fletcher Hollis, a young Black man of Smyrna (age given as 20, 22 or 23), the target of the posses; Black residents of Smyrna whose quarter and houses were searched.

Accused of shooting Constable James D. Wright while resisting arrest; the arrest was on charges of shooting at a man in Dover and creating a disturbance at the Friendship (Mt. Friendship) colored camp meeting.
Posses of armed white men from Smyrna and Clayton led by Smyrna Chief of Police Benjamin Turner, Policeman Joseph Cummins and Constable Charles H. Jones, with W. D. Venn and William King of Clayton.
Hollis was not caught by the posses; sentenced to five years, one hour in the pillory, $500 and costs.
